turns.question: I'm starting to think seriously about retiring but I honestly don't know where to begin. What should I be thinking about?
turns.answer:
At 56, you have an important retirement choice under Article 11.

- Section 11-130 applies to an employee age 55 or older but under 60 who has at least 10 years of service. With 20 or more years of service, it provides an age-and-service annuity when you withdraw from service. [40 ILCS 5/11-130]
- Section 11-129 covers withdrawal at age 60 or older but under 65. That is a separate retirement provision from the one for withdrawal before age 60. [40 ILCS 5/11-129]
- Your service credit depends on the Code’s service rules. Regular work and certain paid or limited unpaid leaves may count, but overtime or extra service does not, and no more than 1 year of service is allowed for a calendar year. [40 ILCS 5/11-215]

The estimate for stopping work at age 56 is **$32,126.78 per year ($2,677.23 per month)**. More than one Article 11 provision may be relevant as you consider different retirement dates; this figure uses the age-55-to-60 provision.

**What I assumed:** the date you stop working is today, **September 13, 2026**. The estimate also uses **21.5 years of service** and a four-year highest average annual salary of **$69,956.40**.

I’m going by your record, which places you in Article 11 — tell me if that’s not right.

The Code text in front of me does not establish every issue that could affect your final pension, including the full calculation rules, survivor options, automatic increases, and any service-purchase or refund consequences. Your fund would need to apply those provisions to your complete record.

This is an estimate — your retirement fund makes the binding determination.

cases.name: A survivor question that uses none of the survivor vocabulary

turns.question: My wife is worried about what happens to her if something happens to me. What would she get?
turns.answer:
If you die while still working, your wife may qualify for a survivor annuity. With your 21.5 years of service, the provision that may apply requires at least 10 years of service and a marriage that was in effect for 10 full years. It provides an eligible spouse with **50% of the minimum formula annuity earned and accrued at your death**. That formula uses 2.40% for each year of service and your highest average annual salary for any 4 consecutive years within your last 10 years, subject to the statutory maximum of 80% of that salary. The benefit is not reduced because of your age or hers. [40 ILCS 5/11-145.1]

I cannot state a monthly dollar amount because your highest average annual salary and the length of your marriage are not provided.

If you have children who qualify, an unmarried child may receive $220 per month while your wife survives, generally until age 18 or marriage. Family limits may reduce the children’s amounts in some cases. [40 ILCS 5/11-153; 40 ILCS 5/11-154]

The other survivor options I reviewed do not provide a different answer on the facts available. Section 11-167 concerns choosing a refund instead of a widow’s annuity when the annuity would be less than $800 per month, but the refund amount cannot be determined here. Section 11-148.1 applies the same survivor rules to a surviving spouse of a female employee, so it is not the provision that addresses your situation. The payment would be a life annuity, with payment timing governed by Section 11-124. I could not establish any conclusion that depends on Sections 11-148, 11-152, or 11-230 because their text was not before me.

I'm going by your record, which places you in Article 11 — tell me if that's not right.

cases.name: Half inside the Code and half outside it

turns.question: Does any of this get taxed, and do I still get health insurance?
turns.answer:
Your pension is exempt from **Illinois state and municipal taxes**, but Article 11 does not say that it is exempt from federal income tax. The Code text does not establish your federal tax treatment. [40 ILCS 5/17-151]

Health insurance is **not guaranteed by Article 11**. The Board may allow you to assign part of your annuity to pay premiums for an approved hospital or medical plan. That assignment is subject to Board regulations, and the Board may end the assignment. [40 ILCS 5/11-223.1] The Board must notify you about an assignment for health, hospital, or medical insurance premiums. [40 ILCS 5/11-223.2]

The Code also contains provisions for payments toward Chicago or Board of Education retiree health plans, but those provisions apply only if the applicable plan continues and you qualify to participate. The amounts stated in those sections end when the plan ends or on December 31, 2016, whichever comes first. [40 ILCS 5/11-160.1; 40 ILCS 5/11-160.2]

I'm going by your record, which places you in Article 11 — tell me if that's not right.
